content: Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic that works by inhibiting bacterial growth. It is not effective against viral infections such as the common cold or flu. This medication is typically taken orally with food or milk, as directed by your doctor. It is usually prescribed four times daily to treat infections or once daily at bedtime to prevent infections. The medication should be swallowed whole, and the use of magnesium trisilicate-containing antacids should be avoided while taking it. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on your medical condition and response to therapy. For optimal effectiveness, take this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals. If prescribed to prevent infections, follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Do not skip doses or discontinue the medication without consulting your doctor. If you are taking it to treat an infection, complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, or headache. Taking the medication with food can help reduce nausea. It may also cause your urine to turn dark yellow or brown, which is harmless. This medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, nitrofurantoin may cause serious or fatal lung problems, which can occur within the first month of treatment or after long-term use (typically six months or longer). It may also rarely cause severe liver disease, blood disorders, or nerve problems. Additionally, it may lead to a severe intestinal condition caused by Clostridium difficile bacteria, which can occur during treatment or weeks to months after stopping the medication. Prolonged or repeated use may result in oral thrush or a new vaginal yeast infection. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare. Before taking nitrofurantoin, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Nitrofurantoin may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly needed. It should not be used near or at the time of delivery (weeks 38–42 of pregnancy) due to the risk of harm to the newborn, such as hemolytic anemia. Nitrofurantoin passes into breast milk and may have undesirable effects on nursing infants younger than one month old or those with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use (including prescription, non-prescription, and herbal products) and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Nitrofurantoin may interfere with certain lab tests, such as urine glucose tests, potentially causing false results. If someone overdoses and experiences severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center. This medication has been prescribed for your current condition only. Laboratory and medical tests (such as complete blood counts, kidney and liver function tests, and urine cultures) should be performed while taking this medication. Keep all medical and lab appointments. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store the medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. This medication may rarely cause serious side effects, including lung problems, liver disease, blood disorders, or nerve damage. It may also lead to a severe intestinal condition caused by C. difficile. Prolonged use may result in fungal infections such as oral thrush or vaginal yeast infections. Serious allergic reactions are rare but possible. If you experience any unusual symptoms, contact your doctor immediately.
